slides.title: The grid: frequency + voltage
slides.body:
An AC grid is a HUGE machine running at a precise frequency (60 Hz in Americas + parts of Asia + Korea, 50 Hz elsewhere). All generators are SYNCHRONIZED. The grid frequency is the canonical signal: too LOW = demand exceeds supply; too HIGH = supply exceeds demand.

**Active power balance**: generation - load = stored kinetic energy in spinning machines.
- Imbalance → frequency drift.
- 60.0 Hz nominal. ±0.1 Hz normal. ±0.5 Hz alarm. ±1.0 Hz disconnects.

**Frequency control**:
- **Inertia**: spinning mass of generators + motors stores kinetic energy. As frequency drops, slows them → releases kinetic energy → SLOWS the drop. Buys time (~seconds).
- **Primary control (governor)**: each generator senses frequency + adjusts output. Responds in seconds.
- **Secondary control (AGC, Automatic Generation Control)**: ~30-second timescale. Restores frequency to 60 Hz.
- **Tertiary control (dispatch)**: minutes-hours. Operator decides what plants to commit.

**Voltage control**: maintained locally via reactive power (VARs).
- Transformers, capacitors, FACTS devices, generator excitation, inverter reactive support.
- Voltage drops along transmission lines (losses + reactance).

**N-1 contingency planning**: grid must survive loss of any single component (a generator, a transmission line, a substation). Multiple-contingency planning for higher-risk regions. Sets operating margins.

**Why this matters for renewables**:
- **Solar + wind have NO inherent inertia**: just power electronics + no spinning mass. Adding more inverter-based generation reduces total grid inertia.
- **Variability**: solar + wind vary on minute-hour timescales. Requires balancing reserves.
- **Geographic concentration**: solar farms cluster in sunny + open areas. Often far from load.

**Grid services from renewables (modern inverters)**:
- **Frequency response**: power electronic response in milliseconds. FASTER than spinning-mass inertia.
- **Voltage support**: reactive power.
- **Black-start capability**: emerging via grid-forming inverters.
- **Primary frequency response**: many inverters now configurable for this.

slides.title: Transmission + distribution + losses
slides.body:
**Transmission**: high-voltage lines (115-1000+ kV AC, or HVDC) carrying bulk power over long distances.
- Higher voltage = lower current = lower I²R losses for same power.
- Modern lines: 765 kV AC + 800 kV HVDC + 1100 kV HVDC (Ultra-HVDC).
- Underground transmission: 5-10× more expensive than overhead. Used in cities + crossing water.

**Distribution**: lower-voltage local lines (4-25 kV typically) delivering to homes + businesses.
- Step-down transformers at neighborhood substations.
- Residential at 120/240 V (USA) or 230/400 V (Europe).

**Losses**:
- Generation → consumption: ~6-10% total losses.
- Transmission: 2-4%.
- Distribution: 4-6%.
- Higher in older grids (India ~20%+) due to infrastructure + theft.

**HVDC (High-Voltage Direct Current)**: alternative to AC for long-distance.
- Lower losses (no reactive component, no skin effect).
- Long submarine cables (AC can't go > ~80 km due to capacitive losses).
- Asynchronous interconnects (link grids of different frequencies).
- Cost: expensive end-station converters; cheap line.
- Crossover ~600 km overhead, ~50-80 km submarine.
- Largest: 1100 kV Zhundong-Wannan in China (12 GW).

**Smart grid**:
- **AMI (Advanced Metering Infrastructure)**: smart meters with two-way comms. ~50% USA deployment.
- **SCADA**: real-time monitoring of grid state.
- **PMU (Phasor Measurement Units)**: GPS-time-synced voltage + current measurements. Wide-area situational awareness.
- **Distributed Energy Resources (DERs)**: rooftop solar, EV chargers, batteries. Aggregated via VPPs (Virtual Power Plants).
- **Demand response**: customers reduce consumption on signals. EV charging schedulers, smart thermostats, industrial loads.

**Grid-forming inverters**: emerging technology. Traditional 'grid-following' inverters need an external voltage reference. Grid-forming inverters CREATE the reference themselves — can operate islanded + start a grid from black-out. Critical for high-renewable grids.

**The 'duck curve'** (CAISO, California): net-load curve in high-solar grids. Solar peaks midday + drops at sunset; load is steady-to-rising. Net load drops sharply during day, then RAMPS UP at sunset. Requires storage + flexible generation to manage. Battery storage is the dominant solution being deployed.

slides.title: Renewable integration challenges + solutions
slides.body:
**Capacity vs energy**: high renewable PENETRATION vs high renewable SHARE are different.
- 100% capacity = renewable nameplate equals peak demand. Doesn't matter when it's calm + dark.
- 100% energy = ALL energy on annual basis from renewables. Needs storage + flexibility.

**The duck curve + storage**: solar-heavy grids need 2-6 hours of storage daily for peak shifting. Battery storage cost-effective at scale.

**Seasonal mismatch**: wind blows more in winter; solar more in summer. Annual storage (multi-month) currently economically infeasible at scale — would need ~petajoules of capacity. Hydrogen + ammonia + long-duration storage emerging.

**Curtailment + negative prices**: when too much renewable on grid, prices go negative + plants paid to stop. ~5% of California solar curtailed in 2023 peaks. Encourages over-building storage + flexible loads.

**Capacity firming**: pair variable renewables with storage + flexible generation (gas peakers, demand response) for reliable supply.

**Transmission needs**: renewable resources often FAR from load. USA: Great Plains has best wind + sun but lowest population. Needs new transmission. Slow due to permitting + NIMBY.

**Examples of high-renewable grids**:
- **South Australia**: ~70% wind + solar share. Has had whole days at 100% renewables. Storage + interconnects to other states critical.
- **Denmark**: ~50% wind. Imports/exports + Norway hydro for backup.
- **Iberia (Spain + Portugal)**: high solar + wind. Limited inertia issues seen.
- **California**: ~30% renewable energy. Battery storage scaling rapidly.
- **Iowa, Texas**: ~30-40% wind. Coal + gas backup.

**Inertia + system-strength concerns**:
- Texas Feb 2021: extreme cold + grid stress. Multiple gas + nuclear plants tripped. ERCOT came close to total blackout. Drove discussion of grid hardening.
- South Australia 2016 'system black': storm + cascading trips. Recovered with grid-forming inverter expansion + storage.

**Future: 100% renewable grid?**
- Technically possible with current technology.
- Requires: massive overbuild of solar + wind, ~10× current storage, transmission expansion, smart loads + sectoral coupling (EVs, heat pumps, electrolyzers as flexible loads).
- Cost trajectory favorable: continued cost declines in solar + storage. 
- Political + permitting challenges + infrastructure speed are the bottlenecks.

question.question: Compute duck-curve storage need
question.goal: Sunny midday: 5 GW solar surplus over load. From sunset to 9 PM peak: load rises 8 GW above solar output (sun is gone). Storage needed to bridge this?

steps.prompt: Surplus during sunny midday: 5 GW for 6 hours = ?
Storage to shift midday surplus to evening: need ~24 GWh at appropriate capacity. With 8 GW power capacity, ~3 hours. With 4 GW power, ~6 hours. Cost?

options: At ~\$300/kWh installed, 24 GWh = \$7.2 billion. Power capacity (4-8 GW) + energy capacity (24 GWh) drive cost. California's deployed 8-10 GW of 4-hour batteries (~30-40 GWh) addresses much of the duck-curve need.

steps.reveal: Multi-billion-dollar investment. California has deployed massive 4-hour battery fleets specifically to address duck curve. The investment is paid back via avoided generation + transmission + serves capacity + ancillary services.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Storage GWh} = \text{average shifting need}}$$ The duck curve gets STEEPER as more solar is added; storage requirements grow. California targeting 50% renewable by 2025 has driven explicit storage mandates (SB 700, AB 327). Tesla's Megapack + EnerC + similar systems are deployed at 100s of MW per project. The economic case is clear: cheaper to buy storage than to over-build solar OR keep gas peakers operating on standby.

question.question: High-renewable grids face 'low inertia' challenges. What does this mean + what's the solution?
options: Traditional grids: spinning machines store kinetic energy. As frequency drifts, that mass slows/speeds + provides damping (~seconds of margin). Solar + wind have NO spinning mass. Solution: grid-forming inverters that synthesize inertia electronically + provide faster response than real inertia.
question.explanation: Grid inertia comes from spinning generators. When frequency drops, generators slow → release kinetic energy → slow the drop, buy time for control systems. Solar + wind have NO inherent inertia. As renewable share grows, total inertia drops. Faster frequency events (under-frequency cascades) become possible. Solutions: (1) grid-forming inverters synthesize 'virtual inertia' in software; (2) battery storage provides millisecond response; (3) synchronous condensers (spinning machines, no generation) provide real inertia. Modern grid codes are updating to require these capabilities from new inverter-based generation.

slides.workedSolution: Inertia = spinning mass × frequency². Stores kinetic energy. When frequency drops, mass releases energy → frequency drop SLOWED. Buys time (~seconds) for governors to respond. Solar + wind = inverter-based = no spinning mass. Solutions: grid-forming inverters synthesize inertia digitally; battery storage provides ms response; synchronous condensers add real inertia. Modern grid codes require some of these. South Australia's 2016 black + lessons learned drive this engineering.

Pathway to 80% renewable grid
question.prompt: A state aims for 80% renewable energy by 2035. Walk through the engineering challenges + investments needed.
Explain in two or three sentences why grid-forming inverters are increasingly required for high-renewable grids.
question.rubric: Mentions that traditional inverters are grid-following (need external voltage/frequency reference); high-renewable grids have less spinning mass to provide stability; grid-forming inverters can synthesize a reference internally, providing inertia + voltage + black-start capability electronically; this enables grids approaching 100% inverter-based generation. Standards (IEEE 1547, IEC 61850) are evolving rapidly to mandate these capabilities.
